$comment: Plain-language explanations for findings every ecosystem shares (bot/lib/adapters/findings.ts). Keyed by finding kind. {placeholders} come from the finding's params, its file/line and the plan's targets. Validated by bot/lib/explain.ts; every kind in bot/lib/adapters/kinds.ts must have an entry (test/explanations.test.ts). learnMore links must be official documentation.

secrets.file.plainTitle: A file with passwords or keys ({name})
secrets.file.inPlainWords: This file holds secrets. The tool never edits it and keeps it locked.
secrets.file.whatWeFound: {file} looks like a credentials file (keys, certificates or passwords).
secrets.file.whyItMatters: Secrets must not end up in a diff, a report or an AI prompt. Locking the file makes sure nothing touches it.
secrets.file.whatWillHappen: Nothing. The file is locked by default and the AI may not read it.
secrets.file.ifApproved: The tool still has no step that edits this file, but the lock that guarantees it is removed. Keep it locked unless you have a reason.
secrets.file.ifLocked: Safe choice. The file stays exactly as it is. If the new version needs new keys or settings, add them yourself after the run.
manualSteps: Check whether the target version needs new or renamed keys in this file.
Update it by hand outside the migration (never paste secrets into the plan notes).

secrets.example.inPlainWords: A template for secrets. Usually harmless, kept locked to be safe.
secrets.example.whatWeFound: {file} looks like an example or template for a credentials file.
secrets.example.whyItMatters: It usually has no real secrets, but people sometimes put real values in by mistake.
secrets.example.whatWillHappen: Nothing. It is locked by default.
secrets.example.ifApproved: The tool has no step that edits it, so in practice nothing changes.
secrets.example.ifLocked: Nothing changes. If the new version needs new setting names, update the template by hand.
manualSteps: Make sure the file contains no real secrets.
Add any new setting names the target version needs.

inline-secret.plainTitle: A password or token written in a settings file
inline-secret.inPlainWords: A secret sits in plain text in {file}. If the tool edits this file, the secret shows up in the diff.
inline-secret.whatWeFound: Line {line} of {file} sets a value that looks like a password, token or key: {evidence}
inline-secret.whyItMatters: Settings files are often rewritten during a migration (renamed properties). Every rewrite copies the secret into the diff and the run report, where more people can see it.
inline-secret.whatWillHappen: Nothing is done about the secret itself. Other edits to this file (if any) still go ahead.
inline-secret.ifApproved: Other planned edits to this file go ahead and the secret may appear in the diff. Move it to an environment variable first if you can.
inline-secret.ifLocked: The whole file is kept as it is, including any property renames planned for it. Those renames then become manual work.
manualSteps: Move the value to an environment variable or your secret store (for example ${DB_PASSWORD}).
Rotate the secret if it has ever been committed.

db-migration.plainTitle: Database scripts that must never be edited ({count} in {dir})
db-migration.inPlainWords: These database scripts have already run in your environments. Changing them breaks the database tooling.
db-migration.whyItMatters: Tools like Flyway and Liquibase remember a checksum of every script they ran. If a script changes, the next deploy stops with a checksum error in every environment that already ran it.
db-migration.whatWillHappen: Nothing. The folder is locked by default so no step and no AI fix can touch it.
db-migration.ifApproved: The lock is removed. No step edits SQL on purpose, but an AI fix-up could, and any edit would break deploys with a checksum error.
db-migration.ifLocked: Safe choice. The scripts stay exactly as they are.
manualSteps: If the upgrade needs a schema change, add a NEW migration script by hand.
Never edit a script that already ran.
db-migration.effort: Up to ~30 min (none if no schema change)

native-code.dir.plainTitle: Native code the tool can't upgrade ({count} file(s) in {dir})
native-code.dir.inPlainWords: Compiled C/C++ code or binaries must be rebuilt for {runtime} {target} by a person.
native-code.dir.whatWeFound: {count} native source or binary file(s) in {dir}.
native-code.dir.whyItMatters: Native libraries are built for one specific runtime. If they aren't rebuilt and retested, the app can crash when it loads them on {runtime} {target}.
native-code.dir.whatWillHappen: Nothing. The files are locked so no step edits them.
native-code.dir.ifApproved: The lock is removed, but no step can rebuild native code, so you still need to do it yourself.
native-code.dir.ifLocked: The files stay as they are. The app may still fail at runtime until they are rebuilt for {runtime} {target}.
manualSteps: Run the code paths that load it.

container.plainTitle: The Docker image still uses old {runtime}
container.inPlainWords: Your app's container image still starts from an older {runtime}. The tool doesn't edit Dockerfiles.
container.whatWeFound: {file} line {line} starts from an older {runtime} image: {evidence}
container.whyItMatters: The upgraded app needs {runtime} {target}. If the image keeps the old runtime, the container can fail to start or crash after you deploy, even though the dry run passed.
container.whatWillHappen: Nothing in the dry run. The tool leaves the Dockerfile alone and lists it as follow-up.
container.ifApproved: Nothing changes. The tool never edits Dockerfiles, so you still need to update the image.
container.ifLocked: The dry run isn't affected. After you merge, the image still uses the old {runtime} until someone updates it.
manualSteps: Change the FROM line to a {runtime} {target} image.
Rebuild the image and start it once locally.

ci.inPlainWords: Your CI pipeline still uses an older {runtime}, so it will fail on the upgraded code.
ci.whyItMatters: The tool only changes the project's own build files. CI keeps the old {runtime} until it is updated, so the first pull request with the migration goes red.
ci.whatWillHappen: Nothing in the dry run. The CI file is left as it is and listed as follow-up.
ci.ifApproved: Nothing changes. The tool doesn't edit CI files, so you still need to update the version.
ci.ifLocked: The dry run isn't affected. CI fails after merge until the {runtime} version is set to {target}.
manualSteps: Set the {runtime} version in this CI file to {target}.
Push it in the same pull request as the migration.

tests.none.plainTitle: No tests to prove the upgrade worked
tests.none.inPlainWords: There are no tests, so a pass only means the code compiles, not that it still works.
tests.none.whatWeFound: The project has no test files.
tests.none.whyItMatters: Tests decide pass or fail. Without them a broken feature can still show as PASSED.
tests.none.whatWillHappen: Nothing is changed. The run continues and the result is marked as less certain.
tests.none.ifApproved: You accept that behaviour is unverified. The run can still pass while a feature is broken.
tests.none.ifLocked: Same as approving: there is nothing to lock. It's kept as a follow-up in the report.
manualSteps: Add at least one smoke test ({testHint}).
Re-run the dry run so the test step proves something.

tests.few.plainTitle: Only a few tests ({tests} for {sources} source files)
tests.few.inPlainWords: Most code has no tests, so a pass proves less than usual.
tests.few.whyItMatters: Code without tests can break and the run still shows PASSED.
tests.few.ifApproved: You accept that untested code is only checked by compiling it.
tests.few.ifLocked: Same as approving: there is nothing to lock. It's kept as a follow-up.
manualSteps: Review the diff of untested files carefully.
Add tests for the riskiest paths ({testHint}).
